To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
FGF‐ 2 mitogenic and differentiating activities can be uncoupled by a single amino acid change in the protein.

(i) a single point mutation (S117A) in FGF‐ 2 reduces its mitogenic activity while retaining its differentiation properties, (ii) FGF‐2 interacts with CK2 in vivo and stimulates its activity during G1‐ S transition, and (iii) the FGF‐ 1/2 receptor is not required for FGF‐2 interaction with CK2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of action of FGF‐2 in the nucleus.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of cell growth and proliferation.
the study of basic fibroblasts growth factor (bFGF) and its interaction with its receptors and its intracellular effectors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FGF‐2 has been shown to have both mitogenic and differentiation properties.
FGF2 mitogenic activity is dependent on a specific interaction with CK2, whereas its differentiation activity requires the activation of the MAPK pathway.
FGF-2 is a mitogenic and differentiation factor, which can be uncoupled by a single mutation, and that CK2 is a nuclear effector involved, in part, in FGF-2 mitogenic activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FGF‐1 and FGF‐2 are not only mitogenic, but also have differentiation properties and are able to translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
we have shown that FGF‐1 and FGF‐2 can have different biological effects depending on the type of receptor to which they are bound.
FGF‐ 2 mitogenic activity requires, in addition to activation of cell surface tyrosine kinase receptor and nuclear translocation of the growth factor, activation of nuclear target(s).
The main takeaway from our work is that
FGF‐1/2 mitogenic activity can be dissociated from its differentiation properties, and that CK2 is a novel nuclear target for FGF‐2 involved in its mitogenic activity.
FGF‐ 2 mitogenic activity requires, in addition to its binding to cell surface receptors and translocation to the nucleus, the activation of nuclear targets, at least CK2.
